title: An Inspector Calls: the Birlings and Gerald
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: modern drama, An Inspector Calls
AO1 and AO2: how a writer presents a character

tips.title: One line, one method, one idea
tips.body: For each of the five characters carry one exact line, one method by which Priestley presents them, and one idea they are there to carry. Fifteen items, and any character question is planned before the paper is open.

tips.title: The test they all sit
tips.body: Every character faces the same question: what do you do with the truth once it is in front of you? Birling, Mrs Birling and Gerald want it undone; Sheila and Eric accept it. Any essay on any character can be built round that test.

tips.title: Presents, not is
tips.body: A question that says *how does Priestley present* wants the writer's choices, not the character's personality. Turn every point into a sentence with Priestley as the subject: Priestley gives, Priestley sets, Priestley delays.

tips.title: Contrast is a method the scheme names
tips.body: The June 2024 indicative content lists the developing contrast of Mrs Birling with Sheila and Eric. Put two characters on the same moment and say what the audience sees; it counts as AO2 and it is quick to write.

tips.title: The trap has a shape
tips.body: Mrs Birling condemns the father before she knows he is her son; the audience knows first. If you write about her, name the dramatic irony and say when the audience works it out, or the point stays a plot summary.

tips.title: Gerald is the third way
tips.body: Not the parents, who deny; not Sheila and Eric, who accept; Gerald is honest and changes nothing. He is the character who shows that telling the truth and taking responsibility are different things.

why.matters: A character in a play is not a person but a set of choices a writer made, and the exam pays for seeing the choices. Priestley gives each of the five a link with the girl, a way of confessing it, and a reaction when the pressure is off, and those three things are built to sort them: the two who accept what they did, the three who want it undone. Reading the characters as constructs is what turns a plot summary into an essay, and it is the difference the mark scheme draws between describing a character and analysing how a writer presents one.

examples.title: The interview and the panel
examples.body: A job interview, a police interview and a school inquiry all do what the Inspector does: they put the same question to different people and watch how each answers. What a person says under that pressure, and what they do afterwards, is how they are judged. Priestley builds his characters on exactly that pattern, so an audience that has ever sat on either side of a table already knows how to read them.

examples.title: Every ensemble drama since
examples.body: A family or a group of friends brought together by one event, each with a secret that comes out in turn, is the engine of a great deal of television and film drama. The characters are designed so that their reactions to the same revelation say who they are. Priestley's five, sorted at the end into those who learn and those who do not, are an early and very clean version of the pattern.

steps.title: Arthur Birling: the hard-headed man of business
steps.body:
Priestley gives Birling the first long speech of the play, and everything in it is wrong. He announces that “I speak as a hard-headed business man” (Mr Birling, Act 1), that “The Germans don't want war” (Mr Birling, Act 1), that the Titanic is “Unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable”, and that “A man has to mind his own business and look after himself” (Mr Birling, Act 1). The audience of 1945, watching a man of 1912 forecast the future, has already stopped trusting him before the doorbell rings.

**What he did.** He sacked Eva Smith from his works for helping to lead a strike for higher wages. Asked to see a connection between that and her death, he sees none: he was protecting his business, and the rest was her affair.

**What he cares about.** His standing. He has been Lord Mayor, he reminds the Inspector that he is a public man, and when the story is out his first worry is that “it isn't going to do us much good” (Mr Birling, Act 2). He is the character who most wants the Inspector to be a fraud, and the one most relieved when he seems to be.

**How Priestley presents him.** Through his own words, which the audience knows to be wrong; through his manner of speech, pompous and repetitive; and through contrast, first with the Inspector's directness and then with his own children. He does not change. That refusal is the point of him.

boxes.title: What he says
boxes.body: No war; the Titanic; look after yourself and your own

boxes.title: What he did
boxes.body: Sacked Eva Smith after the strike, and sees no connection

boxes.title: What he wants
boxes.body: His standing kept: the inquest, the Press, the family name

boxes.title: What he learns
boxes.body: Nothing: relief when the Inspector seems not to exist

visuals.alt: Four boxes on Arthur Birling: what he says, what he did, what he wants and what he learns, which is nothing

check.prompt: Why does Priestley make Birling's opening speech so full of confident predictions?
check.solution: Birling's forecasts, no war, an unsinkable ship, steady prosperity, had all failed by 1945, and the audience knows it. Priestley front-loads the speech with them so that the man who will deny all responsibility has already been shown to be wrong about everything else. It is characterisation by dramatic irony.

markScheme.description: So the 1945 audience, knowing every prediction failed, distrusts his judgement before the Inspector arrives

options: So the audience learns the historical background of 1912 that it needs in order to follow the plot and the characters
So the 1945 audience, knowing every prediction failed, distrusts his judgement before the Inspector arrives
So Gerald and Sheila have reasons to feel hopeful about the marriage before the trouble starts
So Eric can show that he is drunk by interrupting his father with a foolish question about war

steps.title: Sybil Birling: rank, prejudice and the trap
steps.body:
Mrs Birling is from a grander family than her husband, and she behaves as though rank were a moral quality. She chairs a women's charity committee, and when a pregnant girl came to it calling herself Mrs Birling, she took the name as an insult and used her influence to have the appeal refused. Questioned, she does not bend: “girls of that class” (Mrs Birling, Act 2) are not her concern, and “I did nothing I'm ashamed of” (Mrs Birling, Act 2).

**The trap.** Pressed on who is to blame, she says the father of the child should be made to answer for it: “It's his responsibility” (Mrs Birling, Act 2). Sheila had warned her when she came in, “You mustn't try to build up a kind of wall between us and that girl” (Sheila, Act 2), and tries to stop her again as the trap closes, but Mrs Birling walks into it. The father is Eric. She has condemned her own son before she knows who he is, and her composure breaks only then.

**How Priestley presents her.** Through the coldness of her language about the girl; through the dramatic irony of the trap, which the audience sees closing a full scene before she does; and through contrast with Sheila, who understands the Inspector, and Eric, whom she has failed to understand at all. Like her husband she does not change, and at the end she is quick to say that the Inspector made her confess to nothing.

rows: Cold about the girl; blames the father; walks into the trap
Denies she confessed to anything; relieved
props.title: Mrs Birling across the evening

visuals.alt: A table of Mrs Birling before the Inspector's visit, under questioning and after he has gone: composed, then cold and trapped, then unchanged

check.prompt: What makes the trap that closes on Mrs Birling an example of dramatic irony?
check.solution: Dramatic irony is the gap between what the audience knows and what a character knows. By the time Mrs Birling insists that the father should bear the responsibility, the audience, like Sheila, has understood who the father is. Every sentence she says against him is a sentence against her son, and she is the last person in the theatre to hear it.

markScheme.description: The audience has worked out that Eric is the father while she is still demanding that the father be punished

options: The Inspector tells the audience in an aside that Eric is the father of the child before he begins to question her about the committee
Mrs Birling knows Eric is the father and blames him anyway to protect the family's name
The audience has worked out that Eric is the father while she is still demanding that the father be punished
Sheila has told her mother that Eric is the father, and she refuses to believe it

steps.title: Sheila: from the ring to the wall
steps.body:
Sheila begins as the daughter of the house, pleased with her ring and teasing Eric for being “squiffy”. Her link is a bad-tempered, jealous complaint that cost Eva Smith her job at Milwards. What separates her from her parents is what she does with the knowledge. She is upset, she takes it seriously, and she says “I'll never, never do it again to anybody” (Sheila, Act 1).

**She understands the Inspector.** Early on she tells her father that “But these girls aren't cheap labour – they're people” (Sheila, Act 1). When her mother comes in she warns her that the Inspector cannot be kept out, “he knows” (Sheila, Act 2); when Gerald's story comes out she listens to all of it and hands back the ring. She sees the trap before her mother does.

**She does not go back.** When the Inspector has gone and the others relax, Sheila refuses the comfort. Her judgement on her parents, “you don't seem to have learnt anything” (Sheila, Act 3), is the audience's judgement too, and Gerald's “What about this ring?” is left unanswered.

**How Priestley presents her.** Through change: she is the character whose language shifts most, from the chatter of the engagement to the plain sentences of the last act. Through her role as the family's conscience, saying on stage what the audience is thinking. And through contrast with both parents.

rows: Someone who knows, real or not
props.title: Sheila, before and after

visuals.alt: A table of Sheila in Act 1 and Act 3: her language, her view of the girl, of the Inspector and of Gerald, each changed

check.prompt: Which change in Sheila does Priestley use to carry the message of the play?
check.solution: Sheila's change is the play's hope. She admits what she did, sees what it meant, and holds on to that when the older generation lets go. Priestley makes the younger characters the ones who learn so that a 1945 audience will see that the future need not repeat 1912.

markScheme.description: She accepts her share of the responsibility and refuses to give it back when the Inspector seems not to exist

options: She decides to leave home and find work in a shop so that she understands girls like Eva
She forgives Gerald for the affair with Daisy Renton and agrees to take back the engagement ring at the end of the play
She realises the Inspector must have been a ghost and persuades the family to believe her
She accepts her share of the responsibility and refuses to give it back when the Inspector seems not to exist

steps.title: Eric: the drink, the money and the anger
steps.body:
Eric is a problem before the Inspector arrives: he drinks too much, and the family knows it. His link is the worst. He met the girl drunk in the Palace bar, forced his way into her rooms, went on seeing her, and when she was pregnant gave her money taken from his father's office, which she refused. His own account is unsparing: “I was in that state when a chap easily turns nasty” (Eric, Act 3).

**Anger, both ways.** He is angry with his father, “You're not the kind of father a chap could go to” (Eric, Act 3), and, when he learns that his mother turned the girl away, angrier still with her. But the anger is not an excuse, and Priestley does not let him use it as one. At the end he stands with Sheila: “I did what I did” (Eric, Act 3), whether or not there was an Inspector.

**How Priestley presents him.** Through what the family says about him before he speaks; through his confession, which is the plainest in the play; and through the contrast between what he did, which is the worst of the five links, and what he learns, which is more than either parent.

boxes.title: Before
boxes.body: Drinks; interrupts; his parents do not know him

boxes.title: His link
boxes.body: The Palace bar, the rooms, the child, the stolen money

boxes.title: His anger
boxes.body: At a father he cannot go to; at a mother who turned her away

boxes.title: His end
boxes.body: Stands with Sheila: what he did, he did

visuals.alt: Four boxes on Eric: before the Inspector, his link with the girl, his anger at both parents, and his refusal at the end to take the easy way out

check.prompt: Eric did the most harm of the five, yet Priestley places him with Sheila among the characters who learn. What does that pairing show?
check.solution: Priestley separates the characters by whether they accept responsibility, not by how much harm they did. Eric did the worst and admits it whole; his parents did less and admit nothing. The pairing with Sheila makes the split generational and moral at once.

markScheme.description: That responsibility is about what you do with the truth, not about the size of the wrong

options: That responsibility is about what you do with the truth, not about the size of the wrong
That Eric is treated more leniently than the other four because he was drunk when he met the girl and cannot be blamed
That Priestley thinks the younger generation can do no wrong
That Sheila has forgiven Eric because he is her brother

steps.title: Gerald Croft: the honest man who changes nothing
steps.body: Gerald is the outsider at the table, richer than the Birlings and older than Sheila and Eric, and Priestley uses him to show a third way of taking the evening: honestly, and without learning.

visuals.problem: Build a paragraph on how Priestley presents Gerald, from the evidence to the point.

steps.text: Evidence first. Gerald met the girl as Daisy Renton in the Palace bar, got her out of it, kept her in a friend's rooms over the summer, and ended it.
steps.note: The facts of the link, in order, from memory: there is no extract to lean on.

steps.text: What is different about his account: he tells it fully, and he is the only one of the five whose link began as a rescue.
steps.note: Contrast is a method. Beside Birling and Mrs Birling, Gerald looks honest.

steps.text: What he does when the Inspector has gone: he is the one who checks with a police sergeant, finds no Inspector Goole, and works out the loophole about the photograph.
steps.note: The plot turns on him twice, and both times he is looking for a way out.

steps.text: What he says to Sheila: “What about this ring?”
steps.note: The quotation does the arguing: he thinks the evening can be undone.

steps.text: The point: Priestley presents Gerald as decent by the standards of his class, and shows that decency without responsibility changes nothing.
steps.note: The paragraph ends on what the presentation is for.

rows: Took the girl out of the Palace bar
A rescue that became keeping her
props.title: Gerald, twice over

visuals.alt: A table of four things Gerald did, what each looked like, and what Priestley shows about it

check.prompt: Which sentence about Gerald makes a point about how Priestley presents him, rather than describing him?
check.solution: The sentence that pairs the honest confession with the eager search for a loophole names two things Priestley does with Gerald and says what the pairing shows. The sentences about the decent young man in the Palace bar, the richer family and the knighthood, and the news from the police force describe him or retell what he does. Presentation is what the writer does with the character; description is what the character is like.

markScheme.description: Priestley gives Gerald the most honest confession and then the most eager search for a loophole, so that decency without responsibility is shown to change nothing

options: Gerald is a decent young man who met Daisy Renton in the Palace bar, found her somewhere to live and looked after her over the summer before ending the affair as kindly as he could
Priestley gives Gerald the most honest confession and then the most eager search for a loophole, so that decency without responsibility is shown to change nothing
Gerald is from a richer family than the Birlings, which is why Mr Birling is so pleased about the engagement and hopes for a knighthood
Gerald comes back at the end and tells the family that there is no Inspector Goole on the police force, which is a relief to them

steps.title: Two generations, one split
steps.body:
By the end of the play the five have sorted themselves into two groups, and the line runs between the generations. Mr and Mrs Birling, and Gerald with them, take the news that there was no Inspector and no suicide as the end of the matter. Sheila and Eric take it as no difference at all: what they did, they did.

**Why the split matters.** Priestley wrote for an audience in 1945 that was about to decide what kind of country to rebuild. The older Birlings are 1912, unchanged and unchangeable. The younger two are the audience's chance. The split is not there to make the parents villains; it is there to show that the lesson can be learned, and by whom.

**Use it as a method.** Contrast is one of the writer's methods the mark scheme names for this play. A paragraph that sets Sheila's refusal beside her father's relief, on the same moment, is doing AO2 work, and it links straight to context.

rows: Real or not, he was right
props.title: The split at the end

visuals.alt: A table contrasting the older generation with Gerald and the younger generation on the Inspector, the girl, the evening and what each stands for

check.prompt: Why does Priestley put Gerald with the older generation at the end, although he is young?
check.solution: Gerald hears the speech and confesses honestly, yet he is the one who finds the loophole and offers the ring back. Priestley sorts the characters by what they do with the truth, and Gerald does what the parents do. Age is the pattern, not the rule.

markScheme.description: Because the split is about who accepts responsibility, and Gerald, like the parents, wants the evening undone

options: Because Gerald is engaged to Sheila and so already counts as part of the family that her parents run and speak for
Because Gerald is the richest person on stage and money is what the older generation wants
Because the split is about who accepts responsibility, and Gerald, like the parents, wants the evening undone
Because Gerald arrives last and so misses the speech that changes Sheila and Eric

steps.title: Who said it, and what does it show?
steps.body:
Match each line to its speaker from memory, then say in one sentence what Priestley uses the line to show. The second half is the part that earns marks.

1. “But these girls aren't cheap labour – they're people”
2. “girls of that class”
3. “You're not the kind of father a chap could go to”
4. “it isn't going to do us much good”
5. “What about this ring?”

Then try the reverse: for each of the five characters, give one line and one method. If you can do that for all five, you have the raw material for any character question.

check.prompt: Who says that the girls are not cheap labour but people?
check.solution: Sheila says it in Act 1, answering her father's account of the strike. It is the first sign that she will take the girl seriously as a person, and it comes before her own link is revealed, which makes her later confession harder for her and more honest.

steps.title: Character as a construct: what the June 2024 mark scheme wanted
steps.body:
The June 2024 question asked how Priestley uses the character of Mrs Birling to explore ideas about social class. The mark scheme's indicative content is the shape of a top answer for any character question.

**AO1, the whole text:** her attitudes and behaviour before and after the Inspector's visit; the revelations about her treatment of the girl and her response to them; her behaviour once he has gone; how she responds to what the others say and do.

**AO2, the methods:** how she is presented through her words and manner of speech; the developing contrast with Sheila and Eric; the dramatic revelation of her direct involvement; the stage directions about her.

**AO3, the ideas:** selfishness and snobbery; differences in social class; the Inspector's ideas about how society could be organised differently; stereotypes of female behaviour.

Notice what is not there: no plot summary, no biography of Priestley, no paragraph on 1912 for its own sake. Every bullet is either something she says or does at a named point, a method by which she is presented, or an idea the character is there to carry. Write the question's character into those three columns and the essay plans itself.

boxes.title: Says and does
boxes.body: Before, during, after: three points across the whole text

boxes.title: Methods
boxes.body: Words and manner; contrast; revelation; stage directions

boxes.title: Ideas
boxes.body: What the character is there to carry, for 1912 and 1945

boxes.title: Not this
boxes.body: Summary, biography, history for its own sake

visuals.alt: Four boxes for planning a character essay: what the character says and does, the methods, the ideas, and what to leave out

check.prompt: A question asks how Priestley uses Mr Birling to explore ideas about responsibility. Which plan matches what the mark scheme rewards?
check.solution: The plan that runs from his speech and the sacking to his relief, through his manner of speech and the contrast with Sheila, to the ideas about self-interest and community covers the three columns of the indicative content: the whole text, methods, ideas. The plans built on the history of 1912, on everything he says quoted in order, and on Priestley's own life are history, quotation without method, and biography, none of which the scheme lists.

markScheme.description: His speech and his sacking of the girl, his relief at the end; his manner of speech and the contrast with Sheila; the ideas about self-interest and community he is there to carry

options: His speech and his sacking of the girl, his relief at the end; his manner of speech and the contrast with Sheila; the ideas about self-interest and community he is there to carry

The history of 1912, the Titanic, the miners and the strikes; then the story of the play told in order from the dinner to the telephone; then what Priestley believed as a socialist and why he wrote the play
Everything Mr Birling says in Act 1, quoted at length, with a comment after each quotation about whether it is right or wrong
Priestley's own life, the war and the broadcasts, and how they made him dislike men like Birling

steps.title: Five characters, one test
steps.body:
Priestley builds his five characters to fail or pass one test: what they do with the truth when it is put in front of them.

- **Mr Birling:** wrong about everything before the Inspector arrives; denies responsibility; wants the Inspector to be a fraud; unchanged.
- **Mrs Birling:** rank as morality; condemns the father of the child before she knows he is her son; unchanged.
- **Sheila:** the conscience of the family; the character who changes most; refuses the comfort at the end.
- **Eric:** the worst of the five links and the plainest confession; stands with Sheila.
- **Gerald:** honest, decent by the standards of his class, and the one who finds the loophole; changes nothing.
- **The method to name:** contrast, between the generations and between the Inspector's directness and the family's evasions.

For each character carry one line, one method and one idea, and the essay is planned before you open the paper.

check.prompt: Which character is the first to say that the Inspector might not be a real police inspector?
check.solution: Sheila. Priestley gives the first doubt to the character least likely to use it as an excuse, so that when her parents and Gerald seize on it the audience already knows the doubt was never the point.

markScheme.description: Sheila

questions.prompt: What was Eva Smith's link with Mr Birling?
questions.solution: She was one of his workers, helped lead a strike for higher wages, and was sacked when it failed. The link with Milwards is Sheila's and the committee is Mrs Birling's: five characters, five different links, in the order of the girl's life.

markScheme.description: She worked at his works, helped lead a strike for higher wages, and was sacked

options: She was a maid in his house and was dismissed for breaking a plate at the engagement dinner
She worked at his works, helped lead a strike for higher wages, and was sacked
She worked at Milwards and served Sheila, who complained about her
She applied to his charity committee for help and was refused

questions.prompt: Which character chairs the charity committee that refused the girl help?
questions.solution: Mrs Birling, Sybil, chairs the women's charity committee. The girl came to it pregnant, calling herself Mrs Birling, and Mrs Birling used her influence to have the appeal refused.

markScheme.description: Mrs Birling

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes how Sheila reacts when she learns what her complaint at Milwards did?
questions.solution: Sheila is shaken and says she will never do it again to anybody. It is the first confession in the play that admits harm was done, and it separates her from her father, who has just denied that his sacking had anything to do with the girl's death.

markScheme.description: She is upset, takes it seriously, and says she will never do it again

options: She denies that a complaint from a customer could get anyone dismissed
She blames the shop manager for taking the complaint too seriously
She is upset, takes it seriously, and says she will never do it again
She says the girl deserved it for smiling at her in the dress department

questions.prompt: Which character does Priestley present as changing least across the play?
questions.solution: Mr Birling is the same man at the last curtain as at the first: wrong, confident, and concerned for his standing. Sheila changes most; Eric changes; the Inspector does not change because he is not there to.

markScheme.description: Mr Birling, who ends the evening as certain of himself as he began it

options: Sheila, who ends the evening exactly as pleased with her ring as she began it
Eric, who is drunk at the start and drunk at the end
The Inspector, who says the same thing to every character
Mr Birling, who ends the evening as certain of himself as he began it

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs Birling's insistence that the father of the child should be made responsible turn against her?
questions.solution: The father is Eric. Mrs Birling demands that he be dealt with severely while the audience, and Sheila, already know who he is. Priestley builds the trap so that her rank and her rules condemn her own family.

markScheme.description: Because the father is Eric, so every demand she makes is made against her own son

options: Because the father is Eric, so every demand she makes is made against her own son
Because Mr Birling admits that he was the father and that he paid the girl to keep quiet
Because the father is the Inspector himself, which is why he knows so much
Because the Inspector reveals that the father is Gerald, who is engaged to her daughter

questions.prompt: Which of the five characters is the only one whose link with the girl began as a rescue?
questions.solution: Gerald. He took the girl out of the Palace bar and gave her somewhere to live, and Priestley makes the rescue real before showing what it became: keeping her over the summer, then leaving her with nothing.

markScheme.description: Gerald

questions.prompt: What does Eric do when the Inspector has gone and the others decide there was no suicide?
questions.solution: Eric refuses the comfort. The money was still taken and the girl was still treated as he treated her, and he says so. Priestley pairs him with Sheila so the split at the end is between generations.

markScheme.description: He stands with Sheila and says that what he did, he did, whether or not there was an Inspector

options: He apologises to his parents and agrees that the whole evening was a hoax played on the family by a stranger
He stands with Sheila and says that what he did, he did, whether or not there was an Inspector
He leaves the house to look for the girl and find out whether she is alive
He telephones the police himself to report the stolen money

questions.prompt: Which method does Priestley use to make Birling look foolish before he has done anything wrong in the play?
questions.solution: The predictions are the method. The audience knows the Titanic sank and the war came, so Birling is wrong before the Inspector arrives, and his later denial of responsibility comes from a man already shown to have no judgement.

markScheme.description: Dramatic irony: his predictions about the Titanic and the war, which the audience knows failed

options: Stage directions describing him as a small man in a large chair
A soliloquy in which he admits that he does not understand his own children
Dramatic irony: his predictions about the Titanic and the war, which the audience knows failed
The Inspector's arrival at the door, which interrupts him while he is boasting to Gerald about his hopes of a knighthood

questions.prompt: Which pair of characters does Priestley set in the sharpest contrast on the same moment at the end of the play?
questions.solution: The same news, no Goole and no suicide, is a relief to Birling and nothing at all to Sheila. Priestley puts the two reactions side by side so the audience sees the split, and a paragraph that sets them together is using contrast as a method.

markScheme.description: Sheila, refusing the comfort, and Mr Birling, relieved that there was no Inspector

options: Eric and Gerald, who both want the engagement to go ahead as though nothing had happened that evening
Mrs Birling and the Inspector, who argue about the committee
Sheila and Eric, who disagree about whether the girl existed
Sheila, refusing the comfort, and Mr Birling, relieved that there was no Inspector

questions.prompt: Gerald hears the whole of the Inspector's case and confesses honestly, yet he ends the play offering Sheila the ring again. What does Priestley show through this?
questions.solution: Gerald can tell the truth and still want the evening undone. The ring is the sign: he thinks nothing has changed. Priestley uses him to show that decency, by the standards of his class, stops short of responsibility.

markScheme.description: That honesty about the past is not the same as accepting responsibility for it

options: That honesty about the past is not the same as accepting responsibility for it
That Gerald has learned the lesson and wants to make a fresh start with Sheila
That Sheila was wrong to return the ring, since Gerald was the least guilty
That the engagement was never real and Gerald was only after the Birling money

questions.prompt: The June 2024 mark scheme lists 'the stage directions regarding Mrs Birling' as a method. Why do stage directions count as one of the writer's methods in a play?
questions.solution: A stage direction is a choice by the writer about tone, movement, pause or manner, and it changes what a line means. Naming one, and saying what it does, is AO2. The examiners list it because students forget that a play is written to be performed.

markScheme.description: Because a playwright controls how a line is delivered and how a character moves, and those choices create meaning as much as the words

options: Because the examiners can only mark what is printed, and stage directions are printed
Because a playwright controls how a line is delivered and how a character moves, and those choices create meaning as much as the words
Because stage directions are the only part of a play written in the author's own voice, so they are the only place the writer's opinion of a character can be found
Because stage directions describe the set, and the set tells the audience the date and the place

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses contrast as a method rather than merely noting a difference?
questions.solution: The sentence that sets Sheila's refusal beside her father's relief names what Priestley does, puts the two reactions on the same moment, and says what the audience sees. The sentences about young and old, relieved and not relieved, and different opinions state a difference and stop. Method is the choice plus its effect.

questions.prompt: Which character does the audience hear condemn the father of the child, at length, before she knows who he is?
questions.solution: Mrs Birling. The question is a trap in the same shape as the play's: the audience has already worked out that the father is Eric, so every word she says against him is heard twice, once as her judgement and once as her sentence on her own son.

questions.solution: Evidence, then what is distinctive about it, then what he does when the pressure is off, then the line that reveals him, then the point. The point comes last because it is earned by everything before it.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use the character of Mrs Birling to explore ideas about social class? Write one analytical paragraph that could open an answer to this June 2024 question, covering what she says and does, how Priestley presents her, and the ideas she carries.
questions.solution: Priestley presents Mrs Birling as a woman for whom rank is a moral quality, and uses her to show what that belief costs. Before the Inspector arrives she is composed, correcting her children's manners; under questioning she speaks of the girl as one of “girls of that class”, a phrase whose coldness is the method, because it turns a person into a category and a category into something that cannot have a claim on her. Her manner of speech does not bend as the others' do: “I did nothing I'm ashamed of”, she says, and the flatness of the sentence is her character. Priestley then turns her own rules against her. She insists that the father of the child should answer for it, “It's his responsibility”, while the audience, like Sheila, already knows the father is Eric, so the dramatic irony makes her condemn her son in the language of her class. The contrast with Sheila, who tries to stop her and cannot, shows the generations dividing. Through her Priestley explores class as snobbery, as a refusal of responsibility, and as something the Inspector's idea of one body would replace; and by leaving her unchanged at the end he shows a 1945 audience what would not change on its own.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley present the change in Sheila across the play? Write one analytical paragraph, using the contrast between Act 1 and Act 3, at least two checked quotations, and a sentence on why Priestley wanted a 1945 audience to see a young woman change.
questions.solution: Sheila is the character Priestley changes most, and he does it through her language. In Act 1 she is the daughter of the house, pleased with her ring and teasing Eric for being “squiffy”; the words are light because nothing has weight for her yet. Her link, a jealous complaint at Milwards, is small, and what makes her different is the plainness of her response: “I'll never, never do it again to anybody”. From then on her sentences shorten and harden. She tells her father that “But these girls aren't cheap labour – they're people”, she sees before her mother does that the Inspector cannot be kept out, and she hands back the ring while Gerald is still talking. By Act 3 she is the family's conscience, saying on stage what the audience is thinking, and when the others relax she refuses: “you don't seem to have learnt anything”. The contrast with her parents, who end the evening as they began it, is the method that carries the meaning. Priestley wrote for an audience in 1945 choosing what to rebuild, and Sheila is his evidence that the lesson of the play can be learned, and that it will be the young who learn it.

questions.prompt: A student writes: 'Eric is the villain of the play because he did the worst thing.' What is the better reading of how Priestley presents him?
questions.solution: Eric did the most harm and hides none of it, and Priestley places him with Sheila at the end. The play does not rank the five by damage; it sorts them by whether they accept what they did. A villain would be a character the play lets the audience blame instead of itself.

questions.prompt: Mr Birling's first thought when the story is out is the inquest and the Press. What idea is Priestley using Birling to carry at that moment?
questions.solution: Birling's fear is of being seen, not of what was done. Priestley gives him the inquest and the Press at the moment a girl's death has been laid out, so that the audience sees what his values leave out. It is the idea about self-interest against community, carried by one line.

markScheme.description: That a man who measures everything by his standing cannot see responsibility at all, only exposure

options: That a man who measures everything by his standing cannot see responsibility at all, only exposure

examTechnique.body:
**Character questions are method questions.** The wording is always *how does Priestley use* or *how does Priestley present*, and twelve of the thirty marks are for methods. Every paragraph needs a choice the writer made and its effect, not a description of what the character is like.

**Cover the whole text.** The mark scheme's first AO1 bullet is the character's attitudes and behaviour before and after the Inspector's visit. Three points across the evening, not three points from one scene.

**Contrast is on the list.** The June 2024 indicative content names the contrast of Mrs Birling with Sheila and Eric. Use it for any character: put two on the same moment.

**Ideas last, not history first.** AO3 wants the ideas the character carries, class, responsibility, the generations, connected to what Priestley wanted a 1945 audience to think. A paragraph of 1912 background on its own earns almost nothing.
examinerErrors: Describing what a character is like instead of how Priestley presents them, which stops at the lower levels however accurate it is.
Writing about one scene only, when the scheme asks for the character before and after the Inspector's visit.
Retelling the character's link with the girl as a story rather than using it as evidence for a point.
Missing the dramatic irony of the trap around Mrs Birling, and so presenting her collapse as a plot event rather than a method.
Treating Gerald as one of the young who learn, when Priestley places him with the parents at the end.
Quoting lines from memory that are not in the play, or giving a line to the wrong speaker.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the character as Priestley's device and says what the device is for. It moves across the whole play, before, during and after the Inspector, with a checked line at each point; it names methods, the manner of speech, the contrast, the dramatic irony, the stage directions, and says what each does to the audience; and it ends each paragraph on the idea the character carries for 1912 and for 1945. It sees the pattern that sorts the five, and it can say which side Gerald falls on and why. Nothing is retold that is not then used.
